lessons.title: Context: Youth Violence & Group Psychology
lessons.description: Gang culture, Milgram’s experiment, moral responsibility, and Kelly’s dramatic style.
lessons.content_html:
The World Dennis Kelly Wrote For

DNA was first performed in 2008 at the National Theatre, London, as part of the Connections programme for young people. Dennis Kelly wrote the play during a period of intense public anxiety about youth violence in Britain. Knife crime, gang culture, and so-called “happy slapping” were headline news. Kelly wanted to explore how ordinary teenagers — not hardened criminals — could become capable of terrible things when group dynamics take over.

Understanding this social context is vital for AO3 in the exam. The play does not present its characters as inherently evil. Instead, it shows how fear, loyalty, and the desire to belong can push people into moral catastrophe. Kelly is asking the audience: would you behave any differently?

Key Fact

DNA was first performed in 2008. Kelly wrote it in response to growing public concern about youth violence and gang culture in Britain. The play explores how ordinary teenagers can commit terrible acts under the pressure of group dynamics.

Milgram’s Obedience Experiment

One of the key psychological ideas behind DNA is Stanley Milgram’s obedience experiment (1963). Milgram asked volunteers to give electric shocks to a person in another room whenever they answered a question incorrectly. The shocks were fake, but the volunteers did not know that. An authority figure in a white coat simply told them to continue. Astonishingly, 65% of participants administered shocks up to what they believed was a lethal 450 volts.

Milgram’s findings are directly relevant to DNA. Phil never physically harms anyone himself. He gives calm, quiet instructions — and the group obeys. Like Milgram’s participants, the teenagers in the play follow orders even when they know what they are doing is wrong. The experiment demonstrates that obedience to a perceived leader can override personal morality.

Phil acts as the authority figure — calm, detached, and never raising his voice. The group members are the obedient participants. Cathy, who becomes increasingly violent, represents the small percentage of Milgram’s subjects who showed no reluctance at all. Leah, who questions everything but ultimately does nothing to stop Phil, parallels the participants who felt distressed but continued obeying. Richard, who at the end tries to resist, mirrors those who eventually refused the experimenter’s orders.

Kelly uses this psychological framework to argue that cruelty is not about individual evil but about the structures of power and obedience within a group. This is a crucial AO3 point: the play is a commentary on human nature under authority.

Moral Responsibility and Collective Guilt

A central question in DNA is: who is responsible when a group commits a crime? Kelly deliberately blurs individual responsibility. Every member of the group plays a part in what happens to Adam — some through action, others through silence. The concept of complicity runs through the entire play. Even characters who do not directly participate in the violence are guilty because they choose not to stop it.

This connects to a broader philosophical idea: the diffusion of responsibility. When many people are involved, each individual feels less accountable. In the play, no single character says “this was my fault.” The guilt is spread across the group, which makes it easier for each person to justify their own inaction.

Key Fact

Kelly explores the idea of diffusion of responsibility — when guilt is shared among a group, individuals feel less personally accountable. Every character in the group is complicit in the crime against Adam, whether through direct action or deliberate silence.

Kelly’s Dramatic Style

Dennis Kelly writes in a distinctive style. DNA uses sparse, fragmented dialogue with frequent interruptions and overlapping speech. Characters rarely finish their sentences. This creates a naturalistic sense of how teenagers actually talk, but it also reflects the group’s inability to communicate honestly about what they have done.

The play has no stage directions describing the set in detail. Kelly provides minimal information about the locations — “a street,” “a field,” “a wood” — leaving directors to interpret the spaces. This minimalist approach puts the focus entirely on the characters and their moral choices.

DNA has four acts, each preceded by a short scene between Mark and Jan on a street. These “street” scenes function like a Greek chorus, drip-feeding the audience information and building tension. The main action alternates between a field (where Leah talks to Phil) and a wood (where the group gathers). This three-location structure gives the play a ritualistic, almost mythic quality.

Kelly also withholds key information. The audience never directly sees what happened to Adam. Everything is reported through the characters’ fragmented accounts. This forces the audience to piece together the truth, mirroring the way the characters themselves distort and manipulate the story.

The 2008 Connections Programme

DNA was commissioned as part of the National Theatre’s Connections programme, which commissions new plays specifically for young casts. This means Kelly wrote the play to be performed by teenagers, about teenagers, for a teenage audience. The fact that the characters are roughly the same age as the performers and the audience creates a powerful sense of immediacy. The play asks young people to consider their own capacity for cruelty and conformity.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the AQA Paper 2 Section A exam, you will answer one essay question on DNA. There is no extract — you must write about the whole play from memory. The question is worth 30 marks plus 4 for SPaG. You are assessed on AO1 (argument and evidence, 12 marks), AO2 (Kelly’s methods and their effects, 12 marks), AO3 (context, 6 marks), and AO4 (spelling, punctuation, and grammar, 4 marks). AO2 carries exactly as many marks as AO1, so write about how Kelly builds the play — its four-act structure, its staging, its silences — as well as what it means.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Kelly wrote DNA in 2008 in response to public anxiety about youth violence, gang culture, and the ability of ordinary teenagers to commit terrible acts under group pressure.
  • Milgram’s obedience experiment (1963) is a key contextual reference — it shows how people obey authority even when ordered to cause harm, directly paralleling Phil’s control over the group.
  • The play explores moral responsibility and diffusion of responsibility — guilt is shared, so nobody feels individually accountable.

glossary_terms.definition: Violent or antisocial behaviour carried out by groups of young people, often linked to peer pressure and territorial loyalty.
A 1963 psychological experiment by Stanley Milgram that showed ordinary people would obey authority figures even when ordered to administer apparently lethal electric shocks.
Choosing not to act or speak out against wrongdoing, thereby becoming partly responsible for it.
A social psychology concept where individuals in a group feel less personal responsibility for outcomes because responsibility is shared among all members.
A style of playwriting that strips away elaborate staging, leaving the text and performance to carry meaning.
In ancient Greek drama, the chorus was a group that commented on the action, provided background information, and reflected the audience’s perspective.

lessons.title: Acts 1-2: The Crime & the Cover-Up
lessons.description: What happened to Adam, the group’s panic, Phil’s cover-up plan, and Leah’s monologues.
lessons.content_html:
Act 1: The Crime Is Revealed

DNA opens with Mark and Jan on a street, speaking in short, panicked bursts. Through their fragmented conversation, the audience learns that something terrible has happened to a boy called Adam. The group were bullying him — making him walk across a grille, steal vodka, eat leaves — and things escalated. Someone threw him into a shaft, and he fell. The group believes Adam is dead.

Kelly deliberately withholds the full details of what happened. The audience never sees the incident directly. Instead, it is reconstructed through unreliable, overlapping accounts from Mark and Jan. This technique creates dramatic uncertainty — the audience is unsettled because they cannot be sure exactly what took place.

Key Fact

The group bullied Adam by making him walk across a grille, steal vodka, and eat leaves. The bullying escalated until someone threw Adam into a shaft. The group believes he is dead. Kelly never shows the incident on stage — all information comes from fragmented second-hand accounts.

The Group’s Panic

When the group gathers in the wood, the atmosphere is one of collective terror. John Tate, who was the group’s leader before the incident, tries to maintain control but is clearly out of his depth. He threatens anyone who uses the word “dead” and insists they need to “bond” together. His leadership is based on intimidation rather than competence, and it is already crumbling.

The group’s panic reveals their immaturity. They argue, blame each other, and talk over one another. Nobody takes responsibility. Kelly uses the fragmented, overlapping dialogue to show a group falling apart under pressure — exactly the kind of situation where someone calm and decisive can seize control.

John Tate bans the word “dead” and threatens: “I’m in charge. Everyone is happy. What am I?” His desperate repetition and forced assertions of control show a leader who has lost authority. The group humours him but does not genuinely respect him. When Phil finally speaks and offers a plan, the power shift is instant — John Tate is sidelined without a word of protest. Kelly uses John Tate to show that leadership based purely on aggression collapses the moment a real crisis arrives.

By Act 3, John Tate has left the group entirely and “found God.” This could be read as genuine remorse, or as another form of avoidance — he finds a new authority figure (God) to tell him what to do, just as the group found Phil.

Phil’s Plan

Phil, who has been sitting in silence eating an ice cream while Leah talks at him, suddenly speaks. His plan is chillingly detailed. He tells the group to take a sample of Adam’s DNA from a jumper Adam was wearing, plant it on a fictional “postman” suspect, and create a fake witness account using a man they found living rough in the woods. The plan involves framing an innocent person for a crime that may or may not have been committed.

What makes Phil’s intervention so striking is its calm precision. While everyone else is panicking, Phil thinks logically and strategically. He does not shout or threaten — he simply presents the plan as though it were obvious. The group immediately accepts his authority because he offers them what they desperately want: a way out. Kelly shows that in a crisis, people will follow anyone who appears confident, regardless of the morality of the solution.

Key Fact

Phil’s cover-up plan has three components: (1) take Adam’s DNA from clothing, (2) plant it on a fictional suspect by smearing it on a postman, and (3) use a man living rough as a fake witness. The group frames an innocent person. Phil gains leadership not through intimidation but through calm, strategic thinking.

Leah’s Monologues

Interwoven with the plot are Leah’s long, uninterrupted monologues, delivered to Phil in the field. Phil never responds. Leah talks about bonobos (peaceful apes), the nature of happiness, and what it means to be alive. These speeches seem random, but they carry deep thematic weight.

Leah’s monologues function as the play’s moral conscience. She is the only character who genuinely grapples with the ethics of what the group has done. Her references to bonobos — apes that resolve conflict through affection rather than violence — offer an alternative to the group’s behaviour. But Leah is trapped: she knows the cover-up is wrong, yet she cannot bring herself to defy Phil or leave the group.

Leah describes bonobos as creatures that use empathy and physical affection to resolve disputes, in contrast to chimpanzees (and, by implication, the group) who use violence and dominance. She says bonobos are “our nearest relative,” suggesting that humans have the capacity for peaceful resolution but choose aggression instead. This speech directly comments on the group’s choice to cover up their crime rather than confess. Kelly uses Leah to ask: if even apes can choose empathy over violence, why can’t we?

Phil’s silence during these monologues is itself significant. He offers no response, no comfort, and no moral engagement. His refusal to speak reduces Leah to a voice crying in the wilderness — heard by the audience but ignored by the one person she wants to reach.

Act 2: The Plan in Action

In Act 2, the group executes Phil’s plan. They find the man living rough in the woods and use him as their fake witness. The police believe the story. An innocent postman is arrested. The cover-up appears to work perfectly, and the group begins to feel a grim sense of relief. But Kelly signals that this relief is temporary — Mark and Jan’s street scene at the start of Act 2 reveals growing unease. The foundation for the play’s escalation in Acts 3 and 4 is already being laid.

Cathy, meanwhile, is thriving. She is excited about the cover-up and relishes her role in it. Her enthusiasm for the deception — and later for violence — makes her one of the play’s most unsettling characters. While others feel guilt or anxiety, Cathy feels empowered. Kelly uses her to show that group pressure does not affect everyone equally: some people discover that they enjoy cruelty.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 30+4 mark essay, you need to write about the whole play — not just one scene. Plan three or four clear paragraphs, each covering a different moment or character. Since there is no extract, you must remember key details and short quotations. Even paraphrasing specific moments (“when Phil calmly outlines his plan while eating an ice cream”) counts as evidence for AO1. Embed context (AO3) throughout your paragraphs — do not bolt it on as a separate section.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Acts 1 and 2 establish the central crisis: the group bullied Adam, he fell into a shaft, and they believe he is dead. Phil devises a cover-up plan that frames an innocent person.
  • Phil replaces John Tate as leader not through intimidation but through calm strategic thinking — the group follows him because he offers certainty in a crisis.
  • Leah’s monologues function as the play’s moral conscience, exploring alternatives to violence through her references to bonobos — but Phil’s silence renders her powerless.

lessons.title: Acts 3-4: Escalation & the Ending
lessons.description: Adam found alive, Phil’s darker orders, Cathy’s violence, and the bleak ending.
lessons.content_html:
Act 3: Adam Is Alive

The turning point of DNA comes in Act 3 when the group discovers that Adam is not dead. He survived the fall and has been living in the woods, alone and traumatised. This should be good news — nobody has actually committed murder. But the group’s reaction is the opposite of relief. Adam’s survival threatens the cover-up. If he comes forward, the group will be exposed: they have already framed an innocent postman, and the man living rough has been arrested as a false witness.

Kelly uses this reversal to expose the depth of the group’s moral corruption. Instead of being grateful that Adam is alive, they now see him as a problem to be solved. The cover-up has become more important than the person at the centre of it. This is one of the play’s most devastating insights: once a lie takes hold, the truth becomes the enemy.

Key Fact

Adam is found alive in Act 3, but the group sees his survival as a threat, not a relief. If Adam talks, their cover-up unravels: the framed postman, the false witness, and their own lies will all be exposed. The cover-up has become more important than Adam himself.

Phil’s Darker Orders

Phil’s response to Adam’s survival marks a significant moral escalation. In Act 1, his plan involved deception — framing an innocent person, which is serious but does not directly harm anyone physically. In Act 3, Phil considers a far darker solution. He instructs the group to keep Adam hidden and, it is strongly implied, orders them to kill him.

The exact nature of Phil’s instructions is left ambiguous by Kelly. The audience must infer what happens from the characters’ reactions and the events of Act 4. This deliberate ambiguity is a key feature of Kelly’s writing style. By not spelling out the order, he forces the audience to confront the possibility themselves — and in doing so, makes them complicit in imagining the worst.

Phil’s trajectory across the play mirrors the group’s moral decline. In Act 1, he is a strategist; by Act 3, he is potentially ordering murder. Each act requires a greater moral compromise. The group, having already crossed the line with the cover-up, finds it psychologically easier to take the next step. This echoes the psychological concept of the foot-in-the-door effect — once people have complied with a small request, they are more likely to comply with a larger one.

Kelly also shows that Phil’s power has become self-sustaining. By Act 3, nobody questions him — not because he threatens them, but because they have already invested too much in his leadership to turn back. They are trapped by their own earlier compliance.

Cathy’s Violence

Cathy is the most disturbing character in DNA. While other group members show varying degrees of guilt, Cathy is energised by the situation. In Act 3, she reports back from the woods with visible excitement, describing events in graphic terms. She shows no remorse and appears to enjoy the power that violence gives her.

Kelly uses Cathy to explore the idea that group pressure does not simply force people into immoral acts — for some, it provides permission to reveal impulses that were already there. Cathy thrives in the moral vacuum created by the crisis. She volunteers for the most unpleasant tasks and takes pleasure in them. By Act 4, she has joined a media career, cheerfully discussing the events as though they were an interesting story rather than a moral catastrophe. Kelly suggests that in a society that rewards confident, assertive people, characters like Cathy can succeed precisely because they lack empathy.

Key Fact

Cathy is the only character who actively enjoys the violence and chaos. She shows no guilt, volunteers for the worst tasks, and is excited by events others find horrifying. Kelly uses her to suggest that group pressure can give some people permission to express cruelty they already possessed.

Act 4: The Bleak Ending

The final act of DNA offers no redemption. Mark and Jan’s street scene reveals the aftermath: the group has fragmented. John Tate has “found God.” Danny and the others are on medication for anxiety and depression. Leah has disappeared entirely. Phil sits alone in the field, eating, silent, staring into space. Only Cathy appears unaffected — she has moved into television.

Richard, who has replaced Leah in the field scenes, tries to talk to Phil, mirroring Leah’s earlier attempts. Phil does not respond. Richard asks: “What are you thinking?” Phil says nothing. The play ends on this image of total emotional shutdown.

Kelly deliberately avoids a conventional resolution. Nobody is punished. Nobody confesses. The innocent postman’s fate is unresolved. Adam’s fate is implied but never confirmed. The characters simply move on with their lives, carrying varying degrees of damage. Kelly’s message is deeply pessimistic: society does not automatically correct moral failures. People can do terrible things, avoid consequences, and continue to function.

The replacement of Leah with Richard in the final field scene is particularly significant. The play’s moral conscience has been silenced and replaced by someone who is more naively curious than ethically tormented. Kelly suggests that the capacity for genuine moral questioning (Leah) is rarer and more fragile than passive acceptance (Richard).

Leah’s Disappearance

Leah’s absence in Act 4 is one of the play’s most haunting details. She simply vanishes. Kelly provides no explanation — has she left the group voluntarily, or has something happened to her? The audience is left to speculate. Given the play’s trajectory of escalating violence, her disappearance carries sinister overtones. At the very least, it confirms that the one voice of moral conscience has been silenced, and the group is poorer for it.

Richard’s cheerful report that Cathy is “going into television” while others are on medication creates a bitter irony. The character who showed the least remorse is the one who thrives. Kelly uses this to make a pointed social commentary: in a world that rewards confidence and punishes doubt, moral sensitivity is a disadvantage.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about the ending, resist the temptation to say what “should” have happened. Instead, analyse why Kelly chose this bleak conclusion and what it reveals about his view of society. The best essays will connect the ending to the play’s themes: complicity, diffusion of responsibility, and the failure of society to hold people accountable. Use the ending as evidence for AO3 — Kelly is commenting on real-world patterns of moral avoidance.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Adam is found alive in Act 3, but his survival threatens the cover-up. Phil’s response escalates from deception to implied murder — each act requires a greater moral compromise.
  • Cathy thrives in the crisis, showing no guilt and actively enjoying violence. Kelly uses her to suggest that group pressure can give permission to pre-existing cruelty.
  • The ending offers no redemption: the group fragments, Leah disappears, Phil shuts down emotionally, and Cathy enters television. Nobody is punished, and the play’s moral conscience is silenced.

lessons.title: Character Analysis
lessons.description: Phil, Leah, John Tate, Cathy, Richard, Adam, Danny, Mark and Jan analysed.
lessons.content_html:
Phil

Phil is the most complex and enigmatic character in DNA. For much of the play he is silent, eating food while Leah talks at him in the field. He rarely speaks, and when he does, his words carry enormous weight. Phil’s power comes not from aggression but from detachment — he appears unbothered by the moral chaos surrounding him, which makes the group trust his judgement absolutely.

Phil’s trajectory is one of moral escalation. In Act 1, he devises a cover-up; by Act 3, he is potentially ordering murder. Yet Kelly never shows Phil experiencing guilt, doubt, or satisfaction. His emotional blankness is what makes him so unsettling. By Act 4, Phil sits alone in the field, eating, saying nothing. He has not been punished by the law, but he appears emotionally destroyed — or perhaps he was always this hollow.

Key Fact

Phil leads through calm detachment, strategic thinking, and silence. He never shouts, threatens, or shows emotion. His power lies in appearing unaffected — the group follows him because he seems certain when they are panicking. Kelly leaves Phil’s inner life deliberately opaque, making him both fascinating and deeply disturbing.

Leah

Leah is the play’s foil to Phil. Where Phil is silent, Leah is verbal. Where Phil acts decisively, Leah agonises. Her long monologues in the field — about bonobos, happiness, and the nature of existence — reveal a character who thinks deeply about morality but lacks the courage to act on her convictions.

Leah knows the cover-up is wrong. She tries to engage Phil in moral conversation, desperate for him to acknowledge her and the ethical crisis they face. But Phil never responds. Leah’s tragedy is that she has the moral awareness to recognise what is happening but not the strength to stop it. She is trapped between her conscience and her desire to be close to Phil. By Act 4, she has disappeared — the one voice of moral questioning has been silenced.

Leah’s monologues are addressed to Phil, who never responds. This one-sided relationship mirrors the play’s broader dynamic: moral conscience speaks, but power does not listen. Leah tries increasingly desperate tactics to get Phil’s attention — she mentions killing her pet, threatens to harm herself, and talks about death. None of it works. Phil’s silence reduces her to irrelevance. Kelly suggests that in a group dominated by a strong, amoral leader, moral objections simply go unheard.

John Tate

John Tate is the group’s leader at the start of the play, but his authority is built on bluster. He bans the word “dead,” threatens anyone who challenges him, and insists they need to “bond.” But his panic is visible. When Phil offers a plan, John Tate is instantly sidelined. He offers no resistance because, deep down, he knows he has nothing useful to contribute.

By Act 3, John Tate has left the group and “found God.” This could be read as genuine spiritual conversion or, more cynically, as another form of avoidance — replacing one authority figure (himself) with another (God) to escape the burden of personal responsibility.

Cathy

Cathy is the play’s most disturbing character. She shows no guilt, no hesitation, and no empathy. She is energised by the crisis, volunteers for the most violent tasks, and takes visible pleasure in the group’s darker actions. While others deteriorate, Cathy flourishes — by Act 4, she is going into television.

Kelly uses Cathy to explore the idea that group pressure does not just force people into bad behaviour — it can also liberate pre-existing cruelty. Cathy does not become cruel because of the group; the group gives her permission to be who she already is. Her success at the end is Kelly’s most bitter observation: society rewards confidence and assertiveness, even when those qualities are rooted in a complete absence of moral feeling.

Richard

Richard is a minor character who becomes significant in Act 4. He replaces Leah in the field, sitting next to Phil and trying to talk to him. But Richard is not a moral questioner like Leah — he is curious and chatty, reporting news about the group without apparent distress. His presence highlights Leah’s absence: the play’s conscience has been replaced by something lighter and less troubled.

Adam

Adam is the victim. He is barely a character in the conventional sense — the audience never hears his perspective, and he appears on stage only briefly. He exists as the object around which the group’s moral crisis revolves. Kelly’s decision to keep Adam silent and almost invisible reinforces the play’s central horror: the group has dehumanised him. He is a problem to be managed, not a person to be helped.

Key Fact

Adam barely appears on stage and the audience never hears his perspective. Kelly keeps him silent and almost invisible to show how the group has dehumanised him — he is treated as a problem to be managed rather than a person with feelings and rights.

Mark, Jan, and Danny

Mark and Jan function as a chorus. Their short street scenes at the beginning of each act drip-feed information to the audience. They speak in fragmented, overlapping sentences, finishing each other’s thoughts. Their function is structural: they move the plot forward and build suspense.

Danny, Brian, and Lou are secondary group members who show varying degrees of discomfort with the situation but ultimately comply with Phil’s instructions. Danny is particularly notable because he is described as increasingly anxious and, by Act 4, is on medication. Kelly uses these characters to show the psychological cost of complicity — even those who did not directly commit violence are damaged by their participation in the cover-up. Brian has a breakdown during the play, crying and unable to function, which shows the strain the situation places on ordinary teenagers.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Character questions are common in the AQA modern text exam. Plan your essay around three or four key moments where the character is presented differently or where their significance shifts. For each moment, explain what Kelly is showing the audience and link to a relevant theme or contextual point (AO3). Remember: AO2 is worth 12 of the 30 marks, so write about how Kelly builds the character — the lines he gives them, the moments he stages — as well as what the character reveals about his ideas.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Phil leads through detachment and strategic silence — his power comes from appearing calm when everyone else panics. Leah is his foil: morally aware but unable to act.
  • Cathy thrives in the moral vacuum, enjoying violence and showing no remorse. Kelly uses her to suggest that group pressure can liberate pre-existing cruelty.
  • Adam is barely present on stage, reinforcing the group’s dehumanisation of him. Mark and Jan function as a chorus, drip-feeding information and building suspense.

lessons.title: Structure & Stagecraft
lessons.description: Four-act structure, paired characters, Leah’s monologues, offstage action, and settings.
lessons.content_html:
The Four-Act Structure

DNA has a clear four-act structure, with each act representing an escalation in the group’s moral crisis. Act 1 reveals the crime and introduces the panic. Act 2 shows the cover-up in action. Act 3 introduces the twist — Adam is alive — and the group’s response grows darker. Act 4 shows the aftermath: fragmentation, silence, and no resolution. This structure creates a relentless sense of momentum, with each act raising the moral stakes.

Each act is preceded by a short prologue scene between Mark and Jan on a street. These prologues function like a Greek chorus, drip-feeding information to the audience and establishing the emotional tone before the main action begins. The regularity of this pattern creates a ritualistic quality — the audience comes to expect the street scene and the escalation that follows.

Key Fact

The four-act structure creates relentless escalation: Act 1 (crime revealed), Act 2 (cover-up executed), Act 3 (Adam alive, Phil’s darker orders), Act 4 (aftermath with no resolution). Each act is preceded by a Mark-and-Jan street scene that functions as a chorus prologue.

Paired Characters

Kelly structures his characters in pairs that mirror or contrast each other. Phil and Leah are the central pair: Phil is silent and powerful, Leah is verbal and powerless. Mark and Jan are a functional pair who speak in overlapping fragments, almost as a single voice. John Tate and Phil represent contrasting models of leadership — bluster versus strategy.

The most significant pairing shift occurs in Act 4, when Leah disappears and Richard takes her place in the field with Phil. This substitution is Kelly’s way of showing that moral conscience (Leah) has been replaced by passive curiosity (Richard). The play’s emotional centre has shifted from anguished questioning to empty chatter. This structural choice reinforces the bleak message: the capacity for genuine moral reflection is rare and easily lost.

Mark and Jan always appear together, never individually. They finish each other’s sentences and seem to share a single consciousness. Their overlapping, fragmented speech mimics the way teenagers actually communicate, but it also serves a dramatic purpose: by splitting the narrative between two speakers, Kelly makes the information feel uncertain and unreliable. The audience cannot be sure they are getting the full truth.

Their street scenes are placed outside the main locations (field, wood), giving them a detached perspective. They report on events rather than participating in them, which positions them as the audience’s link to the story — they know approximately what we know, and their growing unease mirrors our own.

Leah’s Monologues

Leah’s monologues are a distinctive structural feature of DNA. They are long, uninterrupted speeches delivered to Phil in the field. Phil never responds. The monologues cover seemingly unrelated topics — bonobos, the nature of happiness, whether chimps or humans are more violent — but they all connect thematically to the play’s central concerns about morality, empathy, and what it means to be human.

Structurally, the monologues create a dramatic pause between the tense wood scenes. They slow the pace and invite the audience to think about the broader implications of the group’s actions. Kelly uses them to embed philosophical ideas within a fast-moving thriller plot, giving the play intellectual depth beyond its surface narrative.

Offstage Action

One of Kelly’s most powerful structural choices is to keep the most violent and disturbing events offstage. The audience never sees Adam’s fall, the planting of evidence, the arrest of the postman, or whatever happens to Adam in Act 3. All of these events are described or implied through dialogue.

This technique has several effects. First, it creates ambiguity — the audience can never be completely sure what happened, because they are relying on unreliable narrators. Second, it forces the audience to imagine the violence themselves, which can be more disturbing than seeing it staged. Third, it keeps the focus on the group’s psychological reactions rather than on spectacle. Kelly is not interested in shocking the audience with graphic violence; he is interested in how ordinary people process and justify terrible acts.

Key Fact

Kelly keeps all violent events offstage. This creates ambiguity (the audience relies on unreliable accounts), forces the audience to imagine the worst, and keeps the focus on the characters’ psychological responses rather than on spectacle.

The Three Settings

The play alternates between three locations, each with its own function and atmosphere:

  • The street — Mark and Jan’s prologue space. Public, exposed, transitional. Information is exchanged here but no decisions are made.
  • The field — Phil and Leah’s private space. A place of reflection (Leah’s monologues) and emotional isolation (Phil’s silence). By Act 4, it becomes a space of total emptiness.
  • The wood — the group’s meeting place. Hidden, enclosed, secretive. This is where decisions are made, plans are hatched, and moral lines are crossed. The wood’s associations with darkness and concealment mirror the group’s moral descent.

The three locations can be read symbolically. The street is the public world — normal, everyday life continuing around the crisis. The field is the inner world — Leah’s moral struggle and Phil’s emotional blankness. The wood is the hidden world — where the group’s darkest actions take place, concealed from society. The pattern of moving between these spaces suggests that the characters exist between public normality and private horror, never fully belonging to either.

Kelly gives almost no stage directions for these locations. This minimalism forces the audience to focus on the characters and their words rather than on visual spectacle. It also gives directors enormous creative freedom — the wood could be literally or metaphorically dark, the field could feel exposed or isolated.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions about structure are common in the AQA modern text exam. When discussing structure, always link it to meaning and effect. Don’t just describe the four-act structure — explain why Kelly chose it and what it achieves. For example: “Kelly uses the four-act structure to create relentless escalation, with each act raising the moral stakes and making the group’s position more indefensible.” Structural analysis earns strong AO1 marks when linked to argument.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four-act structure creates relentless moral escalation, with Mark-and-Jan street prologues functioning as a chorus that builds suspense.
  • Kelly keeps all violence offstage, creating ambiguity and forcing the audience to imagine the worst — the focus stays on psychological responses, not spectacle.
  • The three settings (street, field, wood) each serve a distinct dramatic function: public information, private reflection, and hidden group action.

lessons.title: Key Themes
lessons.description: Guilt, responsibility, leadership, power, morality, peer pressure, silence, and complicity.
lessons.content_html:
Guilt and Responsibility

Guilt in DNA is not evenly distributed. Kelly creates a spectrum of responses: Leah is consumed by moral anxiety, Phil shows no visible guilt at all, and Cathy feels nothing but excitement. Danny and Brian develop anxiety and depression. John Tate seeks refuge in religion. The range of responses is Kelly’s way of asking: does feeling guilty matter if you still do nothing to make things right?

The concept of diffusion of responsibility is central to the play. Because the crime is collective, no individual feels personally accountable. Each member can point to someone else: “I wasn’t the one who pushed him” or “Phil told us to do it.” Kelly shows that shared guilt is not the same as shared remorse — the group distributes the blame but nobody actually takes responsibility.

Key Fact

Kelly presents guilt as a spectrum: Leah agonises, Phil shows nothing, Cathy feels excitement, Danny develops anxiety. The concept of diffusion of responsibility means nobody feels individually accountable, even though every member is complicit.

Leadership and Power

The play examines two models of leadership. John Tate leads through intimidation: he shouts, threatens, and demands obedience. His leadership collapses the moment a real crisis arrives because bluster cannot solve practical problems. Phil leads through detachment and strategy: he listens, thinks, and provides clear instructions. The group follows Phil not because they fear him but because he offers them what they desperately need — a plan.

Kelly’s exploration of power connects directly to Milgram’s obedience experiment. Phil is the authority figure in the white coat; the group members are the willing participants. The play suggests that in any group, people will gravitate towards whoever appears most confident and competent, regardless of the morality of their decisions. Power flows to those who provide certainty.

A key debate is whether Phil is a manipulator who deliberately exploits the group’s fear, or simply a pragmatist who sees what needs to be done and does it. Kelly leaves this ambiguous. Phil never lies to the group or flatters them; he simply presents his plan as the logical solution. But the result is the same as manipulation: the group does what Phil says without questioning the morality of his instructions. Whether Phil intends to exploit them or not, the effect of his calm authority is to override their individual moral judgement.

Morality and Amorality

Kelly raises the question of whether morality is innate or learned — and whether it can be abandoned under pressure. Most characters in the play have some sense that what they are doing is wrong, but this awareness does not translate into action. Leah knows, but cannot act. Danny knows, but obeys. Even John Tate, who leaves the group, does not confess — he simply removes himself.

Phil and Cathy represent two forms of amorality. Phil appears to have no moral framework at all — he treats the crisis as a puzzle to be solved, not a wrong to be righted. Cathy, meanwhile, actively enjoys the transgression. Both characters function without a conscience, but for different reasons: Phil through emotional shutdown, Cathy through the pleasure of power.

Peer Pressure and Conformity

The group in DNA is held together not by friendship or loyalty but by fear of exposure. Each member knows that if one person confesses, they all go down. This creates a form of mutual entrapment — the group cannot disband because each person holds information that could destroy the others. Peer pressure in the play is not about wanting to be liked; it is about survival.

Kelly connects this to real-world conformity. Once the group has committed to Phil’s plan, dissenting becomes almost impossible. To speak out would mean admitting personal guilt, betraying the group, and facing consequences alone. The social cost of telling the truth is higher than the moral cost of staying silent.

Key Fact

The group is held together by mutual entrapment, not friendship. Each member knows that confessing would expose everyone. Dissenting means admitting guilt, betraying the group, and facing consequences alone. Kelly shows that the social cost of truth can be higher than the moral cost of silence.

Silence and Complicity

Silence operates on multiple levels in DNA. Phil’s literal silence in the field scenes shows his emotional detachment. The group’s collective silence about their guilt enables the cover-up to continue. Leah’s eventual permanent silence (her disappearance) represents the death of the moral voice. Adam’s silence — he barely appears and never speaks in a meaningful way — represents his dehumanisation by the group.

Kelly uses silence to explore complicity. The play argues that doing nothing is itself a moral choice. Every character who stays silent enables the cover-up. Even Leah, who speaks constantly, is ultimately complicit because her words never translate into action. Kelly’s message is clear: silence and inaction are not neutral — they are active contributions to injustice.

Phil’s silence is strategic — he speaks only when he has a plan, and his silence gives his words greater weight. The group’s silence is self-protective — they stay quiet to avoid consequences. Leah’s silence (when it finally comes, through disappearance) is defeat — she has given up trying to be heard. Adam’s silence is imposed — he is silenced by the group who treat him as an object. Each form of silence serves a different dramatic purpose, but all contribute to the play’s central argument that silence enables moral catastrophe.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Theme questions require you to track an idea across the whole play, not just describe it in one scene. Structure your essay chronologically: how does Kelly introduce the theme, develop it, and resolve (or fail to resolve) it? Always link themes to specific characters and moments. For AO3, connect themes to context: for example, link peer pressure to Kelly’s response to 2008 youth culture, or link silence and complicity to real-world patterns of moral avoidance.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Guilt is presented as a spectrum from anguish (Leah) to absence (Phil and Cathy). Diffusion of responsibility means nobody feels individually accountable.
  • Leadership flows to whoever provides certainty. Phil’s detached strategy replaces John Tate’s bluster, showing that competent amorality can be more dangerous than incompetent aggression.
  • Silence and complicity are active moral choices. Kelly argues that doing nothing is itself a contribution to injustice — every silent character enables the cover-up.

lessons.title: Exam Technique
lessons.description: AQA modern text essay technique: no extract, AO1 and AO2 weighted equally, quotation strategies, model paragraph.
lessons.content_html:
The Modern Text Essay: What Examiners Reward

Modern text essay questions on DNA ask you to write about how Kelly presents a theme, character, or idea across the whole play. You will usually be offered a choice of two questions and must answer one in full.

Crucially, modern text papers are typically closed book and do not provide an extract. You must write about the whole play from memory. This makes the modern text essay one of the most demanding parts of your literature course, because everything depends on what you can remember. On AQA Paper 2 Section A the 30 marks are split AO1 12, AO2 12 and AO3 6, with a further 4 marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Key Fact

A strong modern text essay on DNA delivers four things: a sustained, personal response to the play supported by references from memory; analysis of Kelly’s methods — the four-act structure, the staging, the silences — and the effects they create; context (Milgram, 2008 youth violence, moral philosophy, Connections programme) embedded in your analysis; and clear, fluent academic writing.

What Each Strand of Your Essay Needs to Do

Argument and response: Have a clear thesis and support it with textual evidence. Maintain an analytical style throughout — every paragraph should develop your reading of the play. Kelly’s methods are part of that argument: AO2 carries 12 marks, so say what his choices — the four-act structure, the silences, the field they keep returning to — actually do to an audience.

Context: Show understanding of the relationships between the text and the contexts in which it was written. For DNA, this means: Kelly’s response to 2008 youth violence, Milgram’s obedience experiment, gang culture, moral philosophy, and the National Theatre Connections programme. Context must be embedded in your analysis, not bolted on as a separate paragraph.

Writing quality: Use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose, and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation. This rewards clear, fluent academic writing.

Naming a device (“Kelly uses a metaphor…”) earns nothing on its own. AO2 rewards analysis of the effect a choice creates, so discuss Kelly’s structural and dramatic choices — staging, silence, the four-act structure, the field as a recurring space — and explain what each one does to an audience. Treat every observation about method as an opportunity to say more about meaning; a technique checklist with no meaning attached still earns nothing.

Quotation Strategies for a Closed-Book Exam

Since you do not have the text in front of you, you need practical strategies for incorporating evidence. You do not need to memorise long quotations. Examiners reward relevant references to the play, which can take several forms:

  • Short quotations (1–4 words): These are the most effective for a closed-book exam. Examples: Phil’s “silence,” Leah’s “bonobos,” John Tate banning the word “dead,” Cathy becoming “more and more extreme” after Phil retreats
  • Paraphrased references: Describe a specific moment accurately. Example: “When Phil calmly outlines his plan while eating an ice cream, Kelly contrasts his detachment with the group’s panic.”
  • Structural references: Refer to the play’s form and design. Example: “The replacement of Leah with Richard in the final field scene shows that the play’s moral conscience has been silenced.”
Key Fact

For a closed-book exam, memorise short quotations (1–4 words) and specific moments. You do not need long quotations. Examiners reward accurate paraphrased references to the play just as much as direct quotation. Aim for 2–3 key references per paragraph.

Essay Planning: The 5-Minute Plan

Assume you have around 45 minutes for the modern text question. Spend the first 5 minutes planning. A strong plan should include:

  • Thesis: One sentence stating your overall argument. Example: “Kelly presents guilt as widespread but ultimately meaningless, because no character translates their guilt into action.”
  • 3–4 paragraph topics: Each covering a different character, moment, or aspect of the play. Aim for chronological coverage (early play, middle, end) to show whole-text knowledge.
  • Key references: 2–3 short quotations or specific moments for each paragraph.
  • Context links: One context point per paragraph (e.g., Milgram, 2008 youth culture, Connections programme).

Model paragraph (for the question: “How does Kelly present ideas about guilt in DNA?”):

“Kelly presents guilt as something that is felt but never acted upon, suggesting that moral awareness without courage is ultimately meaningless. Leah is the character most consumed by guilt, delivering long monologues in the field about bonobos — apes who resolve conflict through empathy rather than violence — as an alternative to the group’s behaviour. However, Phil’s refusal to respond renders her moral questioning powerless. Leah knows the cover-up is wrong, yet she never defies Phil or leaves the group. Kelly may be drawing on Milgram’s 1963 obedience experiment, which showed that most people will follow immoral instructions when an authority figure takes charge: Leah, like Milgram’s distressed participants, continues to comply despite her visible anguish. Her disappearance in Act 4 confirms that in Kelly’s world, the voice of conscience is silenced, not because it is wrong, but because it lacks the power to be heard.”

What this paragraph does well: It opens with a clear point about the theme. It uses a short keyword reference (“bonobos”) and a paraphrased moment (Phil’s silence, Leah’s disappearance) rather than long quotations. Context (Milgram) is embedded naturally, not bolted on. It ends with analysis of Kelly’s wider message.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

The most common mistakes in the modern text essay are:

  • Retelling the story: The examiner knows the plot. Every sentence should analyse, not describe. Use “Kelly presents…” or “Kelly suggests…” rather than “Then Phil says…”
  • Bolting on context: Do not write a separate paragraph about Milgram or 2008. Weave context into your analysis: “Kelly, writing in 2008 during a period of intense public anxiety about youth violence, uses Phil’s calm detachment to show how…”
  • Technique-spotting: You can mention dramatic choices (structure, staging, dialogue style) to support your argument, but do not write paragraphs about “Kelly uses a metaphor to…”
  • Only writing about one part of the play: You must show knowledge of the whole text. Reference events or characters from at least three different parts of the play.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Time yourself: 5 minutes planning, 35 minutes writing, 5 minutes checking SPaG. Write 3–4 developed paragraphs, each making a clear point, supporting it with evidence, and linking to context. Quality matters more than quantity — a focused, well-argued essay of 3 paragraphs will outscore a rambling essay of 5. Use the opening sentence of each paragraph to signal your argument to the examiner.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Paper 2, Section A: one essay question on DNA, 30+4 marks, no extract. AO1 (12 marks) and AO2 (12 marks — Kelly’s methods) carry equal weight, with AO3 (6 marks) for context and AO4 (4 marks) for SPaG.
  • Memorise short quotations (1–4 words) and specific moments. Paraphrased references are just as effective as direct quotation in a closed-book exam.
  • Plan for 5 minutes, write 3–4 analytical paragraphs, embed context within your analysis, and avoid retelling the plot or bolting on separate context paragraphs.
